steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our robotics paper LONER, a real-time LiDAR-only SLAM system that learns a neural implicit scene representation. Explain why NeRF-style maps are useful for robotics, position it against existing neural SLAM work, list our contributions, and give the paper outline.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Neural implicit scene representations like Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) are a promising new way of representing maps for robotics applications. A traditional NeRF uses a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to estimate the radiance and the volume density of each point in space, which makes dense scene reconstruction and novel view synthesis possible. This learned representation has several advantages compared to conventional map representations such as point clouds and occupancy grids. First, the domain of the NeRF is continuous and doesn't enforce discretization, so you can query any point in the scene for occupancy. This continuity can be used to solve many different robotics problems. For example, prior work showed that a motion planner can integrate the volume density along a proposed trajectory to evaluate how likely a collision is. Another benefit is being able to produce realistic renders of the scene. NeRFs can also be used to estimate the uncertainty of renders, which enables view selection for active exploration. In this paper we advance neural implicit scene representations for robotics applications. We introduce the first real-time LiDAR-only SLAM algorithm that gets accurate pose estimation and map reconstruction and learns a neural implicit representation of a scene.

A number of recent papers have proposed real-time NeRF-based visual SLAM systems that use monocular or RGB-D cameras. These systems perform impressively on indoor scenes. For outdoor environments, prior work has used neural implicit representations for LiDAR to do dense 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis for large-scale scenes. Recent methods have even shown promising results for LiDAR localization and mapping with neural implicit frameworks in large-scale outdoor scenes. But these LiDAR-supervised algorithms do not run in real-time, and real-time is necessary for robotics applications.

- Contributions
  - 1. first real-time neural implicit LiDAR SLAM; adapts to outdoor; accurate online state estimation
  - 2. novel loss function -> faster convergence, more accurate reconstruction than existing losses
- Results
  - LONER runs real-time; trajectories and maps more accurate than baselines
  - Figure 1: reconstruction on Fusion Portable dataset
  - project page https://umautobots.github.io/loner
- Organization: II related work, III LONER, IV evaluation, V conclusion, limitations, future work

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Neural implicit scene representations like Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) are a promising new way of representing maps for robotics applications. A traditional NeRF uses a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to estimate the radiance and the volume density of each point in space, which makes dense scene reconstruction and novel view synthesis possible. This learned representation has several advantages compared to conventional map representations such as point clouds and occupancy grids. First, the domain of the NeRF is continuous and doesn't enforce discretization, so you can query any point in the scene for occupancy. This continuity can be used to solve many different robotics problems. For example, prior work showed that a motion planner can integrate the volume density along a proposed trajectory to evaluate how likely a collision is. Another benefit is being able to produce realistic renders of the scene. NeRFs can also be used to estimate the uncertainty of renders, which enables view selection for active exploration. In this paper we advance neural implicit scene representations for robotics applications. We introduce the first real-time LiDAR-only SLAM algorithm that gets accurate pose estimation and map reconstruction and learns a neural implicit representation of a scene.

A number of recent papers have proposed real-time NeRF-based visual SLAM systems that use monocular or RGB-D cameras. These systems perform impressively on indoor scenes. For outdoor environments, prior work has used neural implicit representations for LiDAR to do dense 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis for large-scale scenes. Recent methods have even shown promising results for LiDAR localization and mapping with neural implicit frameworks in large-scale outdoor scenes. But these LiDAR-supervised algorithms do not run in real-time, and real-time is necessary for robotics applications.

The contributions of this paper are:

- 1. We propose the first real-time neural implicit LiDAR SLAM method. It adapts to outdoor environments and gives accurate online state estimation.

- 2. We introduce a new loss function that converges faster and gives more accurate reconstruction than existing loss functions.

We show that our method, LONER, runs in real-time and estimates both trajectories and maps more accurately than the baselines. Figure 1 shows reconstruction results on the Fusion Portable dataset. The project page is at https://umautobots.github.io/loner.

The rest of the paper is organized like this: Section II reviews related work. Section III describes LONER. Section IV evaluates LONER, and Section V concludes and discusses limitations and future work.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Neural implicit scene representations, such as Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs), offer a promising new way to represent maps for robotics applications [1]. Traditional NeRFs use a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to estimate the radiance and volume density of each point in space, which enables dense scene reconstruction and novel view synthesis. The learned scene representation has several advantages over conventional map representations such as point clouds and occupancy grids. First, because the domain of the NeRF is continuous and does not enforce discretization, any point in the scene can be queried for occupancy. This continuity can be exploited to solve a variety of robotics problems. For example, as shown in [2], a motion planner can integrate the volume density along a proposed trajectory to evaluate the likelihood of a collision. Other benefits include the ability to produce realistic renders of the scene [1]. NeRFs can also be used to estimate the uncertainty of renders, enabling view selection for active exploration [3]. This paper advances neural implicit scene representations for robotics applications. Specifically, we introduce the first real-time LiDAR-only SLAM algorithm that achieves accurate pose estimation and map reconstruction while learning a neural implicit representation of a scene.

Several recent papers have proposed real-time NeRF-based visual SLAM systems using monocular or RGB-D cameras [5,6,7], and these systems show impressive performance on indoor scenes. For outdoor environments, prior work has focused on neural implicit representations for LiDAR that enable dense 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis for large-scale scenes [8,9,10]. Recent methods have even shown promising results for LiDAR localization and mapping with neural implicit frameworks in large-scale outdoor scenes [11,12]. Still, these LiDAR-supervised algorithms do not operate in real-time, which robotics applications require.

The contributions of this paper are as follows:

- 1. We propose the first real-time neural implicit LiDAR SLAM method, which adapts to outdoor environments and provides accurate online state estimation.

- 2. We introduce a novel loss function that leads to faster convergence and more accurate reconstruction than existing loss functions.

We demonstrate that our method, LONER, runs in real-time and estimates both trajectories and maps more accurately than the baselines. Figure 1 shows reconstruction results on the Fusion Portable dataset [4]. A project page is available at https://umautobots.github.io/loner.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section II reviews related work. Section III describes LONER. Section IV evaluates LONER, and Section V concludes and discusses limitations and future work.
